thread.title: Monday Could Have Been a Disaster for Sentiment: Taking Stock -

author: Bloomberg News
title: Monday Could Have Been a Disaster for Sentiment: Taking Stock -
text:
(Bloomberg) -- S&P futures are following through from Monday’s bounce, getting an added jolt from a positive trade headline ("China Is Said to Move on U.S. Car Tariff Cut Trump Tweeted On") in addition to the German investor confidence data that beat expectations -- though in an indication that any and all positive signs are being fully embraced, it comes as the measure still recorded a negative measure of sentiment.
The same could be said for the Huawei CFO arrest situation, which, despite still festering, allowed trade discussions between U.S. Treasury Secretary Mnuchin and China’s Vice Premier Liu to move forward. It’s unclear if much was accomplished, but at least the bulls have something to point to for the sake of open dialogue.
The U.K. is also looking past yesterday and its Brexit drama after employment figures came in above expected. Energy is getting a bit of a relief rally with BP and Shell adding the most to the FTSE’s rise, followed not far behind by global advertising behemoth WPP Plc, which unveiled its new strategy under their new CEO; watch U.S. names Interpublic and Omnicom for any read through.
Others to watch
Google CEO Sundar Pinchai will be testifying in front of the House Judiciary today to defend data collection processes in what ultimately will be viewed as a proxy for the Internet giants (FB, AAPL, NFLX, AMZN) as a whole. We’ll also be watching air lessors in the U.S. after Air Castle cut its outlook post market, though it’s unclear if it will weigh on AerCap or Air Lease An old IPO darling Stitch Fix, which staged an impressive rally earlier in the year when it nearly tripled, has come down considerably in recent months (~50%) and disappointed with its results and outlook post market; Keybanc called net adds "still inconsistent" while Piper cut its PT to a Street Low $20, citing a flattening of implied Q2 active client adds. Shares are down 17% in the pre-market so far. Averting Disaster
At any moment Monday it appeared we could have been on track to finish below the November close in the S&P at ~2,632, removing one of the last technical defenses for the gauge -- this would have been an absolute disaster for sentiment -- the tenuous nature, though, wasn’t reflected in the closing green on your screens, after what we saw as the largest full reversal (from down as much as 1.9% and below the October intraday low) since February.
The tape again inexplicably benefited from the European close, and by most accounts the lift was broad-based across sectors (energy and financials were the biggest laggards), though breadth may have left the bulls wanting.
Way more stocks set eight-week lows than eight-week highs and decliners outpaced advancers for much of the day in both the S&P and Nasdaq, and that’s despite tech leading on the back of Apple and semiconductor strength. The Qualcomm/Apple headlines in the pre-market were just that -- headlines-- and nothing more, according to most of the Street that saw the risks as passing in nature.
And the SOX index finally broke its 3 day declining streak, likely led by a delayed reaction to Broadcom results that were overshadowed by even bigger headline risk in Huawei. B Riley FBR’s Craig Ellis described recent stock behaviors in the most exposed names (AVGO, ADI, QRVO, SWKS) as "efficient" in having priced the appropriate risks, as the market avoided throwing the "baby out with the bath water" situations. Memory makers (WDC, MU) are among the few that didn’t get to participate in the large upswing after a series of cautious calls on the DRAM market by Morgan Stanley and Mizuho.
But the bottom line is that in the absence of any narrative changing data, Huawei (will Wanzhou get bail?) and Brexit (will the EU renegotiate? Is hard Brexit the only way?) remain the focal points. Theresa May’s Brexit speech took the S&P down nearly 30 points while cratering sterling, leaving money flowing to the dollar and other safe haven currencies.
As my colleague John Authers pointed out over the weekend, currency risks are becoming more prevalent among the list of concerns for stocks. The dollar index’s biggest gain in a month Monday sent crude and the energy sector with it, while placing further pressure on the larger corporates with overseas exposure who can only hope for Goldman Sachs’s "Messy Top" scenario to get underway.
Notes From the Sell Side
The semiconductor hits keep coming, with two cautious notes out this morning: 1) Deutsche Bank says its too early to call the bottom on the sector as the SOX remains ~15% above its 5-year average vs the S&P 500 and risk to estimates remain more likely to the downside in the first half, and 2) Goldman Sachs said datapoints were mostly negative after meetings with >25 companies in Asia cross the hardware, semiconductor and IT supply chain. The latter downgrades Versum to a sell and is incrementally negative on Western Digital, Applied Materials, Lam Research, Entegris, Nvidia, and Tokyo Electron.
JPMorgan downgrades a five oil services companies in a 2019 outlook note titled, "Battening Down the Hatches in Prep for a Later Cycle Environment." Ratings are reduced for long cycle stocks with elevated valuations and continued downside risk to out-year estimates or levered balance sheets where the analysts lack confidence in free cash flow generation: Nabors and Superior Energy move to an underweight while Schlumberger, Weatherford, and Core Labs all go to neutral.
Citi upgrades AT&T to a buy after recent share underperformance (shares down 23% year-to-date vs S&P 500 -1.3%) and argues that the company will benefit from the measured promotional environment in wireless in addition to having several levers to support its net debt deleveraging goals for 2019.
